Experiments that changed questions

The room that filled with smoke

If you are alone, you raise the alarm. If those beside you do not react, you probably will not either. A 1968 experiment.

In 1968, John Darley and Bibb Latané asked students to fill in a questionnaire in a room. Shortly afterwards, smoke began to pour in through a ventilation grille.

Alone or with others

When they were alone, three in four participants went out to report it within a few minutes. When they were with two people who, on the researchers' instructions, kept filling in the questionnaire as if nothing were happening, only one in ten reported it. The rest carried on working in the smoke, rubbing their eyes.

This is pluralistic ignorance: in an ambiguous situation, we look to others to judge whether it is serious; if nobody reacts, we conclude it is not, without realising that the others are doing the same. Knowing this helps: if something looks like an emergency to you, act even if nobody else does.

References

  1. Latané, B. y Darley, J. M. (1968). Group inhibition of bystander intervention in emergencies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 10(3), 215–221.
